title: Consolation and desolation
hookLine: what draws you toward God and what drags you away

cards: Two evenings. On one, the drive home is light: a kind word given or received, and the world seems roomy. On the other, everything's gray, people get snapped at, and praying, or trying at all, looks pointless.
It's easy to file these under good days and bad days. Ignatius wouldn't. In his Spiritual Exercises they're more than moods.
They're movements, inner pulls with a direction, and he gives them names. Today's word is the first of the two.

teach.b: First, consolation, from the Latin for comfort, being comforted.
In his Spiritual Exercises, Ignatius describes it as any inner movement that draws the soul toward God: an increase of faith, hope and love, a deep peace, joy that lifts you toward what matters.

Second, desolation, the opposite pull: darkness, restlessness, a drift toward low things, feeling lazy, lukewarm, sad, as if cut off from God. Here's the surprise: consolation isn't the same as feeling good.
Tears of sorrow for something you've done wrong can be consolation, because they turn you toward God.
And a fun, busy week can hide desolation, if it's quietly pulling you away. The question isn't how do I feel. It's which way am I being pulled.
Ignatius gives advice for both, and one rule is blunt: in desolation, never make a change. Don't quit, don't break up, don't move across the country when everything feels dark.

Stay with the decisions you made in a better light, pray a little more, and wait; Ignatius expects it to pass. In consolation, enjoy it, give thanks, and store up strength for the harder days. Fourth, what it means.
In Ignatius's reading, desolation isn't proof God has left.
He says God can allow it, to teach that consolation is a gift, not something anyone manufactures.

teach.h: WHICH WAY AM I BEING PULLED?
teach.b: This week in camp five: contemplation, the four rungs of lectio divina, read, meditate, pray, rest, then the examen, and now consolation. Every one is a way of paying attention.

how: Catholics who make Ignatian retreats or meet with a spiritual director often talk through their consolations and desolations, using Ignatius's rules for the discernment of spirits to make decisions.

o: a prize given to someone who came in second
any inner pull that draws you toward God, even tears
a cheerful mood that comes after a good day

games.q: which way is the pull — tap the pairs.

s: it's any movement toward God, even tears of sorrow. a fun week can hide desolation.
Ignatius advises never to make a change in desolation
stay with decisions made in a better light, pray, and wait.
Ignatius says desolation proves God has left you
he says God can allow it, to teach that consolation is a gift.

games.q: you're in a gray, heavy stretch. praying feels pointless, and you're tempted to quit something you chose carefully a year ago. what does Ignatius advise?
o: make no change; stay with what you decided in a better light.
stop praying until the mood lifts.
games.why: in desolation, never make a change. stay firm, pray a little more, and wait. Ignatius expects it to pass.

practice: The examen asked where God was; this asks about direction, so go back over the last day and find the moment you felt most drawn toward life, toward love, toward God if you believe: that's your consolation.
Then find the moment you felt most pulled away, dragged down, closed in, and name it without judging: that's your desolation.
Notice the direction of each, not just the feeling, and if you pray, bring both to God, the high with thanks, the low with honesty.

wordCard.voice: Consolation. In Ignatius's language, any movement that draws you toward God, even through tears. Its opposite is desolation. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: comfort, consolation. from con-, with, and solari, to comfort.

carryVoice: Your line: notice the pull. A heavy mood is no time for a big decision. That's the week.

sources.ref: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, nos. 313–336 (rules for the discernment of spirits), esp. 316–318, 322
